pos: n. (William Romaine, 1714–1795, rector of St Anne's Blackfriars, the first settled evangelical incumbent in London)
etymology: Norman French Romain, Roman; William, Germanic, resolute protector.
biblical_def: William Romaine was a Hebrew scholar who edited a new edition of the Hebrew concordance before he was thirty, and then became the most hated evangelical clergyman in London. Elected lecturer at St Dunstan-in-the-West, he found the churchwardens refusing to light the church for his evening lecture, so that he preached by the light of a candle he held himself to crowds filling the street. For years he had no settled charge; in 1766 he at last obtained St Anne's Blackfriars and held it for the rest of his life. His trilogy — The Life of Faith, The Walk of Faith, The Triumph of Faith — is a sustained argument that the Christian lives on Christ moment by moment and not on his own attainments. Hab 2:4 and Rom 1:16 are its spine. Gal 2:20 is its centre, the life now lived in the flesh lived by the faith of the Son of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faith as the assent of the mind to the truth of a proposition advanced by another; and evangelical, as consonant to the gospel.
webster_full: FAITH, n. In theology, the assent of the mind or understanding to the truth of what God has revealed. Evangelical, justifying, or saving faith, is the assent of the mind to the truth of divine revelation, with a firm reliance on Christ for salvation.
EVANGEL'ICAL, a. Consonant to the gospel; according to the gospel; sound in the doctrines of the gospel.
LEC'TURER, n. One who reads or pronounces lectures; a preacher in a church, hired by the parish.
scriptures: Hab 2:4
Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: They put out the lights to stop his lecture and he preached holding a candle, which is the man in one picture.
corruption_paragraphs: Romaine's trilogy is written against a specific disease: the believer who, having begun in grace, begins measuring himself by his frames and feelings and so lives on his own evidences rather than on Christ. Gal 2:20 is the cure, because the life it describes is lived by the faith of the Son of God, borrowed daily. Hab 2:4 says the just shall live by his faith, and the tense is continuous.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors flank the book. One makes assurance rest on introspection until the believer is paralyzed; the other drops the examination of the heart altogether and calls presumption faith. Rom 5:1 holds the ground between them, for peace with God follows a justification already accomplished, which is neither a feeling to be worked up nor a question to be perpetually reopened.
roots_summary: Hebrew emunah (H530), faithfulness, faith; Greek pistis (G4102), faith; dikaioo (G1344), to justify.
usage: “the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4) — continuously, not once.
“the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God” (Gal 2:20) — the trilogy's text.
“being justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Rom 5:1) — the ground beneath the frames.

pos: n. (Henry Venn, 1725–1797, vicar of Huddersfield and rector of Yelling, author of The Complete Duty of Man)
etymology: English Venn, from Old English fenn, a marsh; Henry, Germanic, ruler of the home.
biblical_def: Henry Venn was a Cambridge fellow and a noted cricketer who gave up the game on his ordination, saying he would not have it said that the vicar had been bowled out. At Huddersfield from 1759 he found a rough manufacturing parish and left it, twelve years later, with a church too small for its congregation and societies meeting through the villages. His health broke and he moved to the quiet living of Yelling, where he became a father to the young evangelicals of Cambridge, Charles Simeon among them. His Complete Duty of Man of 1763 was written to replace a popular manual of moralism with a book that puts the gospel first and duty second, and it went through many editions. Eph 2:8 and Eph 2:9 give the order he insisted on. Tit 3:5 is the hinge, that salvation is not by works of righteousness which we have done. Mat 5:16 is where the duties then belong.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines duty, in a religious sense, as obedience due to God; and moralist, as one who teaches the duties of life, or a mere teacher of morality.
webster_full: DU'TY, n. That which a person is bound by any natural, moral or legal obligation to pay, do or perform. Obedience; submission.
MOR'ALIST, n. One who teaches the duties of life, or who practices moral duties; a mere teacher of morality.
VIC'AR, n. The incumbent of an appropriated or impropriated benefice.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: He wrote a book on Christian duty whose first half is about what Christ has done, which was the whole argument.
corruption_paragraphs: The book Venn was answering, The Whole Duty of Man, was not wicked; it was a sober manual of Christian morals that assumed the gospel without stating it, and a generation had been formed by it into decent, unconverted churchgoers. Eph 2:8 and Eph 2:9 are the verses it omitted to emphasize: grace, faith, the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast. Duty detached from that is moralism, and moralism produces either despair or pride.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The same mistake is made now with different vocabulary, in preaching that reduces Christianity to practical steps for better living and keeps the cross for Easter. Tit 3:5 forecloses it. And Venn's title keeps the balance the other way too: duty is not optional, and Mat 5:16 expects visible good works. The order is gospel then duty, never one without the other.
usage: “by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8) — the first half of the Complete Duty.
“Not by works of righteousness which we have done” (Tit 3:5) — against the moralists.
“that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — and the second half.

pos: n. (Thomas Scott, 1747–1821, Bible commentator, chaplain of the Lock Hospital, author of The Force of Truth)
etymology: English Scott, a man from Scotland; Thomas, from Aramaic Te'oma, a twin.
biblical_def: Thomas Scott was a grazier's son apprenticed to a surgeon, dismissed, and sent back to tend sheep, who read his way into holy orders while holding something close to Socinian opinions. Curate at Ravenstone beside John Newton at Olney, he set out to correct Newton's enthusiasm and was converted in the attempt. The Force of Truth, published in 1779, is his account of that progress, written as an argument rather than a testimony: he traces, step by step, how following the evidence of Scripture dislodged each error. He served the Lock Hospital in London, helped found the Church Missionary Society, and produced a commentary on the whole Bible that was the standard English family commentary for a century. John Henry Newman credited Scott's writings, humanly speaking, with making him a Christian. Act 17:11 is the method of The Force of Truth. Isa 8:20 its standard. John 8:32 its title in substance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commentary as a comment; exposition; explanation of a book; and conviction, as the act of convincing or compelling one to admit the truth.
webster_full: COM'MENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; illustration of difficult and obscure passages in an author.
CONVIC'TION, n. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge; the state of being convinced.
CANDOR, n. Openness of heart; frankness; sincerity; a disposition to treat subjects with fairness.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
John 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: He set out to argue John Newton out of his enthusiasm and was converted by the argument.
corruption_paragraphs: The Force of Truth is valuable because it is not an emotional narrative. Scott records the propositions he held, the texts that would not fit them, the resistances he put up, and the order in which each position fell. Act 17:11 describes the practice exactly, searching the scriptures daily whether those things were so, and Scott was his own Berean against himself. John 8:32 promises that the truth makes free, and the freedom in his case came slowly and against his will.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It does rebuke a common assumption, that doctrinal change is driven by temperament or social pressure rather than by evidence, so that argument is useless and only experience persuades. Scott is a counter-example and so, by his own testimony, is Newman. 2Ti 3:16 makes Scripture profitable for reproof and correction, which are words about changing a man's mind.
roots_summary: Greek anakrino (G350), to examine; aletheia (G225), truth; eleutheroo (G1659), to make free.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; Acts 17:11.
usage: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — against his own opinions.
“ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32) — the force of truth.
“profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction” (2Ti 3:16) — a man's mind changed by a book.

pos: n. (Richard Cecil, 1748–1810, minister of St John's Bedford Row, London, memoirist of John Newton)
biblical_def: Richard Cecil was the son of a scarlet dyer, an avowed infidel in his youth who tormented his praying mother and was brought back by the sight of her patience and by his own inability to answer the Scriptures. Ordained in 1777, he held St John's Chapel in Bedford Row from 1780, where his preaching drew the thoughtful rather than the crowd; he was an artist and musician of real gifts who gave both up as competitors for his attention. He was a founding member of the Eclectic Society, helped found the Church Missionary Society, and wrote the memoir of John Newton that preserved much of what we know of him. His Remains, published after his death, is a book of pastoral aphorisms still quoted. 1Pe 3:15 was his mother's unspoken argument and his own afterwards. 2Ti 4:2 the duty he discharged for thirty years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines remains as a dead body; also, the writings of an author left at his death; and aphorism, as a precept or principle expressed in few words.
webster_full: REMA'INS, n. plu. The works of an author which are published after his death.
APH'ORISM, n. A maxim; a precept, or principle expressed in few words; a detached sentence containing some important truth.
CHAP'EL, n. A house for public worship; a place of divine service.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
corruption_summary: His mother said nothing and prayed, and the infidel son wrote the memoir of John Newton.
corruption_paragraphs: Cecil's conversion is the standing rebuke to the idea that argument is everything. His mother did argue, and he beat her arguments; what he could not get past was Jas 5:16, the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous person, worked out in a household over years. The dictionary does not set prayer against apologetics — 1Pe 3:15 commands the answer — but it notes which of the two outlasted his cleverness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in his own practice of giving up his painting and his violin, not because art is sinful but because he judged they were taking the place of his work. That judgement is personal and cannot be legislated; Pro 11:30 calls the winner of souls wise, and wisdom here includes knowing what one must put down. 2Ti 4:2 explains why: being instant in season and out of season leaves little room for rivals.
roots_summary: Greek apologia (G627), a defence; energeo (G1754), to be effectual; kerusso (G2784), to preach.
roots_lines: Greek apologia (G627) — an answer, a defence; 1 Peter 3:15.
Greek energeo (G1754) — to be operative, effectual; James 5:16.
usage: “be ready always to give an answer” (1Pe 3:15) — which he could do, and could not refute.
“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16) — his mother's part.
“he that winneth souls is wise” (Pro 11:30) — and lays down what hinders.

pos: n. (Samuel Walker, 1714–1761, curate of Truro, Cornwall, pioneer of parish-based evangelical ministry)
etymology: English Walker, a fuller of cloth; Truro, a Cornish town.
biblical_def: Samuel Walker was a fashionable young curate at Truro, popular at cards and dances, who was converted about 1746 through conversation with his parish schoolmaster and thereafter emptied the assembly rooms of the town. He refused to itinerate, holding that a minister's charge is his parish, and he built instead what later evangelicals copied: a weekly religious society for his converts with written rules, a monthly clerical club for the neighbouring clergy, careful catechizing, and house-to-house visitation of the whole parish. Wesley consulted him and did not take his advice. Walker's pattern — evangelical conviction worked out through the settled parish rather than around it — became the model for Simeon, Venn and the whole Church of England evangelical party. Act 20:28 is the charge he took literally, to all the flock. 1Pe 5:2 is its manner, feeding the flock willingly and not for filthy lucre.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a parish as the precinct or territory committed to the charge of a priest or clergyman; and visitation, as the act of visiting; a judicial visit.
webster_full: P'ARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting; a visit by authority; as the visitation of a bishop.
SOCI'ETY, n. A number of persons united for mutual benefit or religious edification.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
corruption_summary: He would not itinerate and converted a Cornish town by staying in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The eighteenth-century quarrel between itinerants and parish men is usually told as Wesley against the establishment, with the parish clergy cast as obstacles. Walker complicates that. He was as evangelical as Whitefield and held that Act 20:28 binds an overseer to a particular flock, so that crossing into another man's cure without invitation injures the very work it intends. He was not defending privilege; he was visiting every house in Truro.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Both patterns are biblical in their place: Act 8:4 has the scattered preaching everywhere, and 1Pe 5:2 has elders feeding the flock which is among them. The principle to recover is that settled, unglamorous, house-by-house pastoral work is a strategy and not merely the absence of one, and that Heb 13:7 asks us to consider the end of such a man's manner of life.
roots_lines: Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, a bishop; Acts 20:28.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend, to feed; 1 Peter 5:2.
usage: “to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28) — one parish, entire.
“Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2) — among you, Walker pressed.
“considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) — how such a ministry is judged.

pos: n. (Charles Simeon, 1759–1836, vicar of Holy Trinity, Cambridge, for fifty-four years, patriarch of Anglican evangelicalism)
etymology: Germanic Karl, a free man; Simeon, from Hebrew Shim'on, hearing.
biblical_def: Charles Simeon was converted at nineteen while preparing, in terror, for a compulsory college communion, and in 1782 was appointed to Holy Trinity, Cambridge, where the pewholders locked their pews against him and the churchwardens locked the doors on his evening lecture. He preached to people standing in the aisles for years. He held the living fifty-four years and outlasted all of it. He established the Friday evening conversation parties where generations of undergraduates were taught how to read a text and construct a sermon, published the Horae Homileticae of some two and a half thousand sermon outlines on the whole Bible, helped found the Church Missionary Society, sent Henry Martyn out, and created a trust to buy church livings so that evangelical ministers could be appointed after him. 2Ti 2:2 describes the Friday evenings. Act 20:27 is the principle of the Horae, the whole counsel of God, text by text.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines homiletics as the art of preaching; and perseverance, as persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken.
webster_full: HOMILET'IC, a. Pertaining to familiar intercourse; social; conversable; pertaining to the art of preaching.
PERSEVE'RANCE, n. Persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; continuance in a state of grace to the end.
ADVOW'SON, n. In English law, a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
corruption_summary: They locked the pews against him for a decade; he stayed fifty-four years and trained the men who went everywhere.
corruption_paragraphs: Simeon's rule for preaching was that the text must speak and the preacher must not: to bring out of Scripture what is there, and to put into Scripture what is not there, were to him the two capital sins. Act 20:27 is the positive form of that, declaring all the counsel of God rather than a favourite portion of it, and the Horae Homileticae is the discipline applied to every book of the Bible in order.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live failure is topical preaching that uses a verse as a motto for a subject chosen in advance. The other failure, less noticed, is impatience: Simeon endured ten years of organized contempt in his own parish, and the whole evangelical movement in the Church of England stands on his refusal to leave. 2Ti 4:2 pairs preaching with longsuffering for a reason.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit to one's charge; 2 Timothy 2:2.
Greek hupostello (G5288) — to shrink back, to shun; Acts 20:27.
usage: “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the Friday evenings.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the whole Bible, in outline.
“with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2) — ten years of locked pews.

pos: n. (the Eclectic Society, founded in London 1783, a clerical conference of evangelical ministers and laymen)
biblical_def: The Eclectic Society met fortnightly in the vestry of St John's Bedford Row and afterwards at the Castle and Falcon, Aldersgate, from 1783. John Newton, Richard Cecil, Henry Foster and others gathered to put a question — practical, doctrinal or missionary — and talk it through, one man presiding and each speaking in turn. Josiah Pratt's notes of the discussions survive and are among the most useful documents of English evangelicalism, because they catch working ministers thinking aloud. On 18 March 1799 the question was how to spread the gospel among the heathen, and the Church Missionary Society came out of that meeting. Pro 11:30 and Ecc 4:9 are the two plain texts behind such a body, that he who winneth souls is wise and that two are better than one because they have a good reward for their labour. Act 15 is the apostolic pattern of brethren conferring before acting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eclectic as selecting; choosing; and a conference, as the act of conversing on a serious subject; a meeting for consultation.
webster_full: ECLEC'TIC, a. Selecting; choosing; an epithet given to certain philosophers who selected from the opinions and principles of others what they thought solid and good.
CON'FERENCE, n. The act of conversing on a serious subject; a discourse or discussion; a meeting for consultation.
CONSULTA'TION, n. The act of consulting; deliberation of two or more persons on some subject.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
corruption_summary: A fortnightly ministers' conversation in a London vestry produced the Church Missionary Society in one evening.
corruption_paragraphs: The Eclectic model is worth recovering in detail. It was small, regular, unofficial, minuted, and organized around one question at a time, with every man expected to speak. Ecc 4:9 is the practical warrant. What it produced was not resolutions but clarity, and out of clarity, institutions — the Church Missionary Society, and much of the early impulse behind the Bible Society.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern substitute is the conference with a platform and an audience, which is a different thing and does different work. Mat 9:38 commands prayer for labourers; Act 2:42 has a church continuing in doctrine, fellowship, bread and prayers. The principle to recover is that ministers need a place to think together without performing, and that great enterprises usually begin in such rooms.
roots_summary: Hebrew shenayim (H8147), two; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; ekballo (G1544), to send forth.
roots_lines: Greek ekballo (G1544) — to thrust forth, to send; Matthew 9:38.
usage: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9) — the vestry rule.
“he that winneth souls is wise” (Pro 11:30) — the question always before them.
“that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38) — 18 March 1799.

pos: n. (Josiah Pratt, 1768–1844, secretary of the Church Missionary Society 1802–1824, recorder of the Eclectic Society)
etymology: Hebrew Yoshiyahu, the LORD supports; Pratt, from Old English prætt, a trick, used as a surname.
biblical_def: Josiah Pratt was a Birmingham japanner's son, Richard Cecil's curate, and then for twenty-two years the man who actually ran the Church Missionary Society. He took it over when it had no missionaries at all and left it with a worldwide establishment: he recruited Lutherans from Berlin when no Englishmen would go, founded the Missionary Register, devised the system of associations that funded the work from ordinary parishes, and corresponded with every station. He also took the notes of the Eclectic Society's discussions that preserve its debates, and edited an edition of Foxe. He is the type of Christian worker the histories omit, the administrator without whom the preachers go nowhere. Rom 10:15 asks how they shall preach except they be sent, and sending is largely clerical labour: money, ships, letters, lists. 1Co 15:58 is the promise attached to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a secretary as a person employed to write orders, letters and records; and administration, as the executive part of government.
webster_full: SEC'RETARY, n. A person employed by a public body, by a company or by an individual, to write orders, letters, dispatches, public or private papers, records and the like.
ADMINISTRA'TION, n. The act of administering; direction; management; government of public affairs.
REG'ISTER, n. A book in which is recorded any transaction or facts; a list; a record.
scriptures: And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
corruption_summary: Somebody has to find the money, book the passage and answer the letters, and for twenty-two years that was Pratt.
corruption_paragraphs: Rom 10:15 contains a clause the missionary literature tends to hurry past: except they be sent. Sending is a corporate act with a budget, a committee and a correspondence, and a church that honours only the goer has not read the verse. Pratt never served abroad and is responsible, under God, for a great part of what the first generation of Anglican missionaries accomplished.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the unseen office. 1Co 3:6 refuses to rank the planter above the waterer because God gives the increase, and the same refusal covers the man who neither plants nor waters but buys the seed. 1Co 15:58 promises the stedfast and unmoveable that their labour is not in vain in the Lord, and the promise is not restricted to the visible kind.
roots_summary: Greek apostello (G649), to send; kopos (G2873), labour; auxano (G837), to give increase.
roots_lines: Greek apostello (G649) — to send forth with a commission; Romans 10:15.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to preach, to herald; Romans 10:15.
Greek auxano (G837) — to give the increase; 1 Corinthians 3:6.
usage: “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — the clause about committees.
“your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — twenty-two years of letters.
“but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — no ranking among the workers.

pos: n. (John Venn, 1759–1813, rector of Clapham, chaplain of the Clapham Sect, a founder of the Church Missionary Society)
etymology: English Venn, from Old English fenn, a marsh; John, from Hebrew Yochanan.
biblical_def: John Venn was Henry Venn's son, and from 1792 rector of Clapham, where John Thornton had bought the living to secure an evangelical ministry for the village. His parishioners included Wilberforce, Zachary Macaulay, Granville Sharp, Henry Thornton, James Stephen and Charles Grant, and Venn was the pastor of that extraordinary congregation for twenty-one years. He preached plainly and at length against the slave trade to the men who were abolishing it, chaired the meeting that founded the Church Missionary Society in 1799, and drafted its principle that it should follow the leadings of Providence and begin where the door was open. In the parish he founded a school and a society to supply the poor with coal and clothing. He is the quietest man in the Clapham story and the one who fed the rest. Act 20:28 is his office. Jas 1:27 is the religion his congregation practised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rector as a clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish; and philanthropy, as love to mankind; benevolence toward the whole human family.
webster_full: REC'TOR, n. A ruler or governor. A clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish, and has the tithes.
PHILAN'THROPY, n. Love to mankind; benevolence towards the whole human family; universal good will.
BENEF'ICENCE, n. The practice of doing good; active goodness, kindness, or charity.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
corruption_summary: He was the pastor of the men who ended the slave trade, which is a harder job than it sounds and left no monument.
corruption_paragraphs: The Clapham achievements are usually credited to the laymen, rightly, but the laymen were under a ministry. Venn preached to them weekly for twenty-one years, catechized their children, buried their dead and kept the doctrine in front of them while they worked at Parliament and the companies. Act 20:28 charges an overseer with the flock, and a flock of reformers needs feeding like any other.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the relation between pulpit and public action. Jas 1:27 makes visiting the afflicted and keeping unspotted the two halves of pure religion, and the Clapham men did the first because they were being taught the second. Mat 5:16 ties the works to the Father's glory. A congregation that acts without being fed burns out; a congregation that is fed and does not act has not understood the food.
roots_lines: Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, to care for; James 1:27.
usage: “to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28) — that flock.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — what Clapham did.
“that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father” (Mat 5:16) — and why.

pos: n. (the circle of evangelical reformers resident at Clapham, south London, c. 1790–1830)
etymology: Clapham, Old English, the homestead by the hill; sect, from Latin secta, a following.
biblical_def: The Clapham Sect was never a sect and never called itself one; the name was a later joke about a group of Church of England laymen who happened to live around Clapham Common and worship under John Venn. Wilberforce, Henry Thornton the banker, Zachary Macaulay, Granville Sharp, James Stephen, Charles Grant and Hannah More in their orbit pursued, over four decades, the abolition of the slave trade and then of slavery itself, the founding of Sierra Leone, the opening of India to missionaries, prison and factory reform, the Bible Society and the Church Missionary Society. They worked by patient parliamentary labour, bought a newspaper, documented atrocities, and lost repeatedly for twenty years before the trade was abolished in 1807. Jas 1:27 is the shape of the whole. Mat 5:16 is its visibility. Pro 11:30 is the aim beneath the politics, for they were evangelists before they were reformers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abolition as the act of abolishing; an annulling; and reform, as to change from worse to better; to amend.
webster_full: ABOLI'TION, n. The act of abolishing; or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation; utter destruction.
REFORM', v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
PHILAN'THROPY, n. Love to mankind; benevolence towards the whole human family.

Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mat 5:16

corruption_summary: They lost the abolition vote for twenty years and then won, and kept going for twenty-six more until slavery itself fell.
corruption_paragraphs: Clapham is claimed today by people who want the social reform without the doctrine that drove it, and the claim does not survive the documents. These men believed in hell, in the new birth, in the atonement and in the authority of Scripture, and they abolished the trade because they believed Africans were image-bearers with immortal souls for whom Christ died. Jas 1:27 joins visiting the afflicted to keeping unspotted from the world in one sentence, and Clapham refused to separate them.

The opposite error, common among conservative Christians, is to treat political and social labour as a distraction from the gospel. The Clapham men were simultaneously funding missionaries, printing Bibles, and sitting on committees for twenty years without visible result. 1Co 15:58 is the verse for that kind of work: stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding, labour not in vain. Pro 11:30 kept the order right, for they wanted souls first and statutes second, and got both.
usage: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this” (Jas 1:27) — Clapham's programme.
“that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — and they did.
“always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — through twenty lost votes.
